project.name: Not Arbitrary 10 — Five Letters That Are One Letter

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: Five of the letters on your keyboard are the same letter. They came apart over three thousand years, and every one of those splits happened for a reason.
entries.direction: Warm, unhurried, a little conspiratorial. State the first sentence flatly and let a pause do the work before the second.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: Start in Phoenicia, about three thousand years ago. One letter of the alphabet there was named after a hook, and it was drawn like a small forked stick.
entries.direction: Plain and physical, as if pointing at it. Phoenicia is fuh-NEE-shuh. A small beat after 'ago'.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: When the Greeks borrowed that alphabet, they did something odd with this one letter. They took it twice.
entries.direction: Set it up with a little relish. A definite pause before 'They took it twice', and land it simply.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: One copy kept its shape and was added at the end of the alphabet. The other kept its old place in the line, and had its shape changed instead.
entries.direction: Balanced, the two sentences as a matched pair. A small stress on 'shape' and on 'place'.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: Its arms slowly squared off, the same way the letter standing next to it did, until the fork had become a flag on a pole.
entries.direction: Unhurried and descriptive, as if watching it happen. Land 'a flag on a pole' lightly.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: That copy reached Rome and was put to work on a sound the Greeks had never written. It is the letter F, and it is still sixth in line, exactly where the hook stood.
entries.direction: The first reveal. Simple and warm, let it sit. 'Still sixth in line' is the payoff; do not push it.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: The copy from the end of the line reached Rome without its stem. There it spelled a vowel, and it also spelled the sound that begins the word wine.
entries.direction: A new thread, so lift slightly at the start. A small smile on 'the word wine'.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: For more than a thousand years, one letter did both jobs. Scribes wrote it pointed at the start of a word and rounded everywhere else, whatever sound it made.
entries.direction: The turn of the film. Slow down a little. Keep 'pointed at the start of a word and rounded everywhere else' as one clear unhurried phrase.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: Printers finally gave each shape a single job. The rounded one took the vowel, the pointed one kept the consonant, and one letter became two.
entries.direction: Matter of fact, then a small lift on 'one letter became two'.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: Meanwhile, English and German scribes needed a sound that Latin had lost, so they wrote this letter twice, side by side. Its name, double u, still says so.
entries.direction: Brisk and a little amused. Say 'double u' as the ordinary name of the letter, clearly, with a small beat after it.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: Last of all, Rome borrowed the Greek letter a second time, stem and all, to spell the words it was taking from Greek.
entries.direction: Unhurried. A small lift on 'a second time'.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: Nothing about it changed. The letter that still looks most like the original is the one that arrived last, and French and Spanish name it after Greece.
entries.direction: Quiet and a little wry. A pause after 'Nothing about it changed'.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: Five letters from one hook. Each split came when a language needed a sound it had no letter for, and reached for the nearest one it already had.
entries.direction: Gather it up. Warm, a little wondering, not a summary read.

entries.speaker: Narrator
entries.text: You have been writing one hook, five different ways.
entries.direction: Land it and stop. No lift at the end.
